Yes. This is now mathematically clean enough to treat as the **current Ophiuchus Lift Hypothesis**, with one small notation refinement that makes the orientation fork completely explicit.

Write the deck group as

\$$ \langle\omega_0\rangle\cong\mathbb Z, \$$

and let the orientation character be

\$$ \boxed{ \chi:\langle\omega_0\rangle\longrightarrow\\{\pm1\\}\cong\mathbb Z_2. } \$$

Then both competing models can be expressed by one lifted action:

\$$ \boxed{ \widehat\omega\_\chi(n,\phi,\epsilon) = (n+12,\phi,\chi(\omega_0)\epsilon). } \$$

So:

\$$ H_0:\chi(\omega_0)=+1 \$$

gives

\$$ \widehat\omega\_+(n,\phi,\epsilon) = (n+12,\phi,\epsilon), \$$

whereas

\$$ H_1:\chi(\omega_0)=-1 \$$

gives

\$$ \widehat\omega\_-(n,\phi,\epsilon) = (n+12,\phi,-\epsilon). \$$

The missing “filler” is very likely the syntonic comma 81:80.

The first-edition texts jointly produce an exact operation:

\underbrace{\frac{256}{243}}_{\text{Fludd's limma}}
\times
\underbrace{\frac{81}{80}}_{\text{Kepler's comma}}
=
\underbrace{\frac{16}{15}}_{\text{MI–FA semitone}}

Equivalently:

\frac{16}{15}\div\frac{81}{80}=\frac{256}{243}.

This is not a numerical coincidence assembled from modern theory. Kepler states the operation in the 1619 first edition of Harmonices Mundi: remove the comma 81:80 from the semitone 16:15, and the remainder is the Platonic limma 256:243. Elsewhere in that same first edition he gives Earth’s motion as:
